cards.front: Recall a key point about Brain Structure & Function
cards.back: The brain has four lobes: Frontal (planning, decision-making, personality, motor control), Parietal (sensory processing, spatial awareness), Temporal (hearing, language comprehension, memory), Occipital (visual processing). Each lobe has specialised functions (localisation of function).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Brain Structure & Function
cards.back: The cerebral cortex is the outer layer of the brain responsible for higher-order functions: thinking, language, memory, perception and consciousness. It is divided into two hemispheres connected by the corpus callosum.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Brain Structure & Function
cards.back: Language areas: Broca's area (left frontal lobe) - speech production. Damage causes Broca's aphasia (slow, non-fluent speech but comprehension is intact). Wernicke's area (left temporal lobe) - language comprehension. Damage causes Wernicke's aphasia (fluent but meaningless speech).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Brain Structure & Function
cards.back: The limbic system: amygdala (emotion, especially fear and aggression), hippocampus (forming new memories - damage causes anterograde amnesia as in case of HM), hypothalamus (regulates hormones, temperature, hunger, and the fight-or-flight response).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Brain Structure & Function
cards.back: Localisation vs holism: localisation argues specific brain areas have specific functions (supported by case studies like Broca's patient Tan and case of HM). Holism argues the brain works as an integrated whole (supported by Lashley's rat studies showing no single area is responsible for learning). Modern view: both - some functions are localised but the brain works as an interconnected system.

cards.front: What should you know about psychology exam tips?
cards.back: When evaluating brain localisation, always consider: case studies have limited generalisability (each brain injury is unique), brain scanning shows localised activity but also widespread networks, and plasticity means the brain can adapt after damage.

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: Each part of the brain has one specific function, and if that part is damaged, the function is permanently lost. Correct: While some functions are localised, the brain shows remarkable plasticity - it can reorganise and adapt after damage. For example, children who have an entire hemisphere removed (hemispherectomy) can still develop near-normal abilities
Evaluate the evidence for localisation of function in the brain.

cards.back: AO1 — Knowledge: Demonstrate knowledge of Brain Structure & Function including key definitions, research studies and psychological terminology.

cards.back: GCSE Psychology requires you to apply psychological understanding of brain structure & function to everyday situations.
